en: The Jātaka: The Section of Eighty Birth Stories,
Chapter on the Lesser Swan (Cūḷahaṃsavagga)
4. The Kuṇāla Jātaka.
Thus it is declared, thus it is handed down:

[It was] on the bearer of all medicinal herbs, strewn with many flower garlands, frequented by elephants, gavayas, lions, ruru deer, camarī antelopes, spotted deer, khaḍga deer, go-kaṇṇa deer, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, large monkeys, kadali deer, wild cats, sasaka deer, and kaṇṇika deer.

It was frequented by herds of great boars, elephant families, and female elephants; it was inhabited by stags, sākha-deer, sarabha-deer, eṇī-deer, vāta-deer, pasada-deer, and purisāluka-antelopes, as well as kimpurisas, yakkhas, and rakkhasas;

it was overspread with numerous trees bearing clusters of flowers and fruits, dripping with honey and pollen; and it was constantly filled with the cries of flocks of birds such as ospreys, cakoras, vāraṇas, peacocks, parrots, jīvañjīvakas, celāvakas, abhiṅkāras, karavīkas, and intoxicated birds.
In such a delightful forest grove, indeed, O sir, which is adorned with many hundreds of thousands of minerals—
such as antimony, realgar, yellow orpiment, vermilion, silver, and gold— there dwells a bird named Kuṇāla,
who is exceedingly beautiful and possesses most beautiful feathers and wings. Now, O sir, that bird Kuṇāla has three thousand five hundred female bird-maidens as his attendants.
Then, indeed, O sir, two brahmin girls, having taken a stick in their mouths and caused that Kuṇāla bird to sit in the middle,
flew up with him, thinking: "May no fatigue from the journey along the road overcome this Kuṇāla bird."
Five hundred female birds flew up from below, thinking,
"If this bird Kuṇāla should fall from his seat, we shall catch him with our wings.
Five hundred female birds flew up above.
“May the heat not scorch that bird Kuṇāla.
Five hundred and five hundred female birds flew up on both sides [of him], thinking:
“May cold or heat, grass, dust, wind, or dew not touch that bird Kuṇāla.”
Five hundred female birds flew up ahead of him,
crying out: "May cowherds, or shepherds, or grass-gatherers, or wood-gatherers,
or forest-workers not strike this bird Kuṇāla with a stick, or a clod, or a hand, or— with a stone, or a staff, or a sword, or with pebbles!"
“Let this bird Kuṇāla not be obstructed by trees, creepers, branches, pillars, rocks, or even by powerful birds.
Five hundred female birds flew after him from behind, addressing him with words that were gentle, affectionate, charming, and sweet, saying:
“Let this bird Kuṇāla not become weary of his seat.”
Five hundred female birds flew about in every direction, gathering various fruits from many different trees,
thinking, "Lest this bird Kuṇāla be exhausted by hunger.
Then, indeed, those female birds [carried] that bird Kuṇāla from grove to grove and from park to park.
Just as one goes from river-ford to river-ford, from mountain peak to mountain peak, from mango grove to mango grove,
from rose-apple grove to rose-apple grove, from breadfruit grove to breadfruit grove, or from coconut plantation to coconut plantation,
they very quickly reach their destination for the sake of pleasure.
Then, indeed, Master, the bird Kuṇāla, having been surrounded by those daughters of birds throughout the day, reproached them thus:
"Perish, you outcasts! Be destroyed, you outcasts! You are thieves, harlots, unchaste, fickle-minded, and ungrateful for what has been done; like the wind, you go wherever you please.
Now, Master, on the eastern side of that very Himavat, the king of mountains, there is a source of rock from which an extremely fine and subtle [substance] originates.
They enter the groves where blue lotuses,
red lotuses, white lotuses, pink lotuses, hundred-petaled lotuses, and fragrant *sogandhika* lilies grow in abundance, forming beautiful, fragrant, and delightful places.

There are forests of *kuravaka*, *mucalinda*, *ketaka*, *vedisa*, *vañjula*, *punnāga*, *bakula*, *tilaka*, *piyaka*, *hasana*, *sāla*, *saḷala*, *campaka*, *asoka*, *nāga*, *tirīṭi*, *bhujapatta*, *loddha*, and *candana* trees.

In a dense thicket of *kāḷāgaru*, *padmaka*, *piyaṅgu*, *devadāru*, and *kacoca*; where *kakudha*, *kuṭaja*, *aṅkola*, *kaccikāra*, *kaṇikāra*, *kaṇṇikāra*, *kaṇavera*, *koraṇḍaka*, *koviḷāra*, *kiṁsuka*, *yodhika*, *vanamallikā*, *manaṅgaṇa*, *manavajja*, *bhaṇḍi*, *surucira*, *bhaginī*, *mālā*, and *malyadhara* trees grow;

where the ground is strewn with *jāti*, *sumana*, *madhugandhika*, *dhanu*, *takkāri*, *tālīsa*, *tagara*, *musīra*, *koṭṭha*, and *kachava*; and where the region is adorned by the spreading creepers of *atimuttaka* in full bloom.

In such a delightful grove, indeed, O friend—resounding with the cries of swans, water-fowls, ducks, and kāraṇḍava birds; frequented by hosts of *vidyādharas*, *siddhas*, ascetics, and forest-dwellers;

and traversed by noble deities, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *dānavas*, *gandharvas*, *kinnaras*, and *mahoragas*—there dwells a pheasant-parrot named Puṇṇamukha, whose voice is exceedingly sweet, whose eyes are playful, and whose gaze is intoxicated.
Indeed, sir, that Phussakokila with the full face had two hundred and fifty female parrot-maidens as his attendants.
Then, sir, two of those female parrots would take hold of a stick with their beaks, place the Phussakokila with the full face in the middle, and carry him along, thinking:
"May no fatigue from the journey on the road overcome the Phussakokila with the full face."
Fifty female birds flew up from below, one after another, thinking:
"If this Puṇṇamukha, the cuckoo, should fall from his seat, we shall catch him with our wings.
Fifty female birds flew up above, one after another.
“May the sun not scorch this full-faced *phussa* cuckoo,” they thought.
Fifty bird-maidens fanned him from both sides,
thinking, “May cold, heat, grass, dust, wind, or dew not touch this full-faced *phussa* cuckoo.”
Fifty female birds flew up one after another in front of him,
thinking: "Lest cowherds, or shepherds, or grass-gatherers, or wood-gatherers,
or forest-workers should strike this full-faced *phussa* cuckoo with a stick, or a clod, or a hand, or a stone, or a staff, or a sword."
“Or they struck him with pebbles.
May this Puṇṇamukha, the cuckoo Phussa, not encounter strong birds, or branches, creepers, trees, boughs, pillars, or rocks.
Fifty bird-maidens followed behind him, addressing him with words that were gentle, affectionate, charming, and sweet.
“May this full-faced *phussa* cuckoo not become weary upon his seat”;
fifty female birds flew off in every direction, gathering various fruits from many different trees, [thinking]:
“May this full-faced *phussa* cuckoo not be exhausted by hunger.”
Then, sirs, those young female birds led that Puṇṇamukha Phussakokila from grove to grove,
from park to park, from river-ford to river-ford, from mountain peak to mountain peak, from mango grove to mango grove,
from rose-apple grove to rose-apple grove, from breadfruit grove to breadfruit grove, and from coconut plantation to coconut plantation.
They quickly mastered the art of moving like coconut shells for the sake of sport.
Then, indeed, Master, Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo, surrounded by those bird-maidens throughout the day, praised them thus:
"Excellent, excellent, sisters! This is truly worthy of you, daughters of noble family, that you should attend upon your husband."
Then, sirs, the golden-breasted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha approached the bird Kuṇāla.
The young female birds who were Kuṇāla’s attendants saw the golden-breasted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha coming from afar;
having seen him, they approached the golden-breasted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha, and having approached him, they said this to the golden-breasted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha:
“Friend Puṇṇamukha, this bird Kuṇāla is exceedingly harsh and exceedingly foul-mouthed. Perhaps, by coming here, we might obtain some pleasant speech even from him.
“Perhaps so, sisters,” he said, and he approached where the bird Kuṇāla was. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the bird Kuṇāla and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo said this to the bird Kuṇāla:
“Friend Kuṇāla, why do you behave wrongly toward women who are well-born daughters of noble families and who conduct themselves properly?
Friend Kuṇāla, one ought to speak pleasantly even to women who speak unpleasantly, so how much more so to those who speak pleasantly?
When this was said, the bird Kuṇāla rebuked the peacock Phussamukha in this way:
“Begone, friend jackal, outcaste! Perish, friend jackal, outcaste! For what wise man would associate with one like you?
Thus insulted, Puṇṇamukha the peacock immediately turned back from that very spot.
Then, sirs, after no long time, a severe illness arose in Puṇṇamukha the peacock; he was afflicted with dysentery and intense, death-agony pains set in.
Then, sirs, it occurred to the female bird-maidens who were attendants upon Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo:
"This Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo is afflicted with illness; perhaps he might recover from this affliction. Leaving one another in solitude, they approached the place where the bird Kuṇāla was.
The bird Kuṇāla saw those female birds coming from afar; seeing them, he said this to the female birds:
“But where are your husbands, you low-born women?
“My dear Kuṇāla, Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo is indeed afflicted; perhaps he might recover from that affliction.
When this was said, the bird Kuṇāla rebuked those young female birds in this way:

“Perish, you outcasts! Be destroyed, you outcasts! You are thieves, harlots, ungrateful, fickle-minded, and those who do not repay what has been done for them—you go wherever you please like the wind!
Having said this, he approached Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo; having approached, he said this to Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo:
“Hey, friend Puṇṇamukha!”
“Yes, friend, it is Kuṇāla.
Then, Master, the bird Kuṇāla took hold of that Phussakokila with full beak by means of his wings and beak, lifted him up, and made him drink various medicines.
Thereupon, Master, that affliction of the Phussakokila with full beak subsided.
Then, friends, the bird Kuṇāla said this to the peacock Puṇṇamukha, who had recently recovered from illness:
"Friend Puṇṇamukha, I saw Kaṇhā Dvepitikā, while she was setting her heart on a sixth man, even though she already had five husbands, upon a headless trunk and a cripple.
And regarding this, there is a verse: [The verse follows.]
“Then Ajuna, Nakula, Bhimasena,
Yudhiṭṭhila, and King Sahadeva—
these five husbands did she surpass in wisdom, O woman.”
"She committed a sin with a hunchbacked dwarf.
"I have seen it, friend Puṇṇamukha. A female ascetic named Saccatapā, living in the midst of a charnel ground and skipping every fourth meal, committed a sin with a drunken rogue.
"I have seen it, friend Puṇṇamukha. A queen named Kākavatī, living in the midst of the ocean and the wife of Venateyya, committed a sin with Naṭakuvera."
"I have seen it, friend Puṇṇamukha: the doe named Kurungadevī, while longing for a young ram, committed a sin with the disciple of Chaḷaṅgakumāradhana.
Thus was this known by me, [concerning] the mother of Brahmadatta."
Having abandoned the King of Kosala,
he committed evil with Pañcālacaṇḍa;
both he and others committed such evil deeds.
Therefore, I do not trust women, nor do I praise them;
just as the earth is equally attached to all beings in the world,
so too is the bearer of wealth a support for one and another alike.
All things are together, unshakable, and immovable;
a person should not place trust in those who stand thus.
Like a lion that feeds on red flesh, [the wise do not rely on such states].
A wild beast with five weapons, fiercely enraged,
who devours by force and delights in harming others—
such women as these a man should not trust.
"Indeed, my dear Puṇṇamukha, courtesans are not women to be approached; they are not called 'prostitutes,' but rather 'slayers.

For these courtesans are like thieves in their guise, like merchants smeared with wine in their verbal flattery, like lions in their deceitful rolling about, like snakes with forked tongues, like pits in their concealment, like the underworld in their insatiability, and like ogresses in their difficulty to appease."

They are like Yama, carrying away all at once; like fire, devouring everything; like rivers, flowing everywhere; like the wind, moving wherever it desires; like Mount Meru, making no distinctions; and like a poison tree, always bearing fruit. Furthermore, there is this verse on the subject:
They are like Yama, carrying away all at once; Like fire, devouring everything; Like rivers, flowing everywhere; Like the wind, moving wherever it desires; Like Mount Meru, making no distinctions;
And like a poison tree, always bearing fruit. Moreover, there is this further statement regarding this matter:
Like a thief, like one smeared with poison,
like a merchant who boasts,
and like one who turns back from a lion or a bull.
Like a double-tongued serpent, like a hidden pit,
and like an abyss difficult to fill.
Like a rākṣasī, difficult to satisfy;
like Yama, who carries away all at once;
as fire, a river, or the wind.
They come together like a swarm of bees;
like a *visarukkha* tree that is always bearing fruit,
they destroy the wealth in the house.
"Those women who destroy wealth.
"My dear Puṇṇamukha, there are these four things which, when a task arises, become harmful;
they should not be allowed to stay in another's family:"
An ox, a milch cow, a vehicle, and a wife—
a wise person should not let these four riches stay away from home.
An ox, a milch cow, and a vehicle...
One should not leave one's wife to stay with her kinsmen;
for those who lack draft animals break the chariot,
and by over-driving, they kill the lead bull.
The cow kills its calf;
the wife commits adultery with her relatives.
These six things, friend Puṇṇamukha, become harmful when a crisis arises.
A bow without string, a wife in the family of her kinsmen,
a boat without oars, a vehicle with broken axles,
a friend who stays afar, and an evil companion— these are useless.
"When a duty arises, those who act for one's detriment come forward.
Indeed, my dear Puṇṇamukha, there are eight grounds on which a woman despises her husband:
poverty, illness, old age, drunkenness, stupidity, negligence, compliance in all his affairs, and the failure to provide all the wealth."
Indeed, my dear Puṇṇamukha, for these eight reasons a woman despises her husband.
And there is this verse on the subject:
"To one who is poor and also sick..."
The aged, the drunkard,
the negligent, and the foolish—
these cause the neglect of all duties.
"By granting all her desires,
she treats her husband with contempt.
"Indeed, my dear Puṇṇamukha, there are nine grounds on which a woman incurs hatred."
She has the habit of going to pleasure groves; she has the habit of going to parks; she has the habit of going to river fords;

she has the habit of going to her own family circle; she has the habit of going to other families; she has the habit of being devoted to the practice of adorning herself with slave-girls and fine clothes; she is a drinker of intoxicants; she has the habit of gazing [at men]; and she has the habit of standing at the doorway.
Indeed, my dear Puṇṇamukha, it is through these nine grounds that a woman incurs ill repute.
And regarding this, there is further a verse:
"Addicted to pleasure groves and gardens..."
A woman who frequents rivers, kinsmen, and the families of others,
who is devoted to mirrors, fine clothes, and ornaments, and who drinks intoxicants— [such a woman is not fit for marriage].
She who is habitually gazing [at men],
and she who stands at the doorway;
by these nine causes, [she is not protected].
"Women bring about ill-will.
"Indeed, friend Puṇṇamukha, there are forty-four ways in which a woman transgresses against a man:
she yawns, she arches her body, she coos, she acts bashfully, she scratches nail against nail, and she kicks foot against foot."
He steps on [something]; he scratches the earth with a stick; he leaps over a child or causes another to leap over one; he plays or causes another to play;
he kisses or causes another to kiss; he eats or causes another to eat; he gives or asks for something; he imitates what has been done;
he speaks loudly, speaks softly, speaks indistinctly, or speaks clearly; [he engages] in dancing, singing, instrumental music, or weeping.
Adorned with playful gestures, she laughs, looks about, wiggles her hips,
shifts her private ornaments, uncovers her thigh, covers her thigh, displays her breast, displays her pubic hair, displays her navel, rolls her eyes,
raises her eyebrows, scratches her lips, lolls out her tongue, and disrobes.
She fastens her garment, releases her head-ornament, and binds her head-ornament—
for indeed, my dear Puṇṇamukha, by these forty grounds does a woman act improperly toward a man.
Furthermore, my dear Puṇṇamukha, by twenty-five grounds a woman should be known as being corrupted.
She praises her husband’s absence; she does not remember him when he has departed; she does not rejoice when he has returned;
she speaks ill of him; she does not speak well of him; she acts for his detriment; she does not act for his benefit;
she does what should not be done for him; she does not do what should be done for him; she sleeps having turned away from him; she lies down with her back toward him.
She has become prone to infidelity and flirtatiousness; she breathes deeply and experiences suffering;
she frequently goes for defecation and urination; she acts perversely; upon hearing the voice of another man, she dilates her ear-cavities;
she has been deprived of her wealth; she cultivates intimacy with neighbors; and she has set out on her way [to meet others].
She wanders through the streets and is indeed unfaithful; she is constantly disrespectful toward her husband and possesses a corrupted intention.
She frequently stands at the door, displaying her armpits, limbs, and breasts, and having gone here and there, she gazes about.
"My friend Puṇṇamukha, by these twenty-five points, a woman should be known as one who is corrupted."
And furthermore, there is this verse on this subject:
"He praises his departure from home;
he does not grieve for him when he has gone."
Having seen him returned, she does not rejoice;
she never speaks words of praise for her husband;
these are the signs of one who is corrupted.
The unrestrained woman pursues what is harmful and neglects her own welfare by failing to do her duty; having scorched him,
she sleeps with her back turned to him.
These are the characteristics of one who is corrupted.
She becomes disfigured and stained with menstrual blood;
she breathes deeply and experiences painful sensations.
She frequently goes to relieve herself of excrement and urine;
these are the signs of one who is corrupted.
She acts contrary to what is right and performs what ought not to be done.
One listens to the speech of another as they speak;
one forms intimacy with those whose wealth has been destroyed—
these are the signs of one who is corrupted.
He squanders with ease the wealth acquired with difficulty and brought together with hardship, which was amassed through suffering;
he cultivates intimacy with his neighbors.
These are the characteristics of one who is ill-disposed.
She walks about outside the house with her feet uncovered,
and she is constantly malicious in mind toward her husband.
She is unfaithful and devoid of respect;
these are the characteristics of one who is corrupted.
She stands constantly at the threshold of the door.
Displaying their private parts and loins,
she gazes in every direction with a distracted mind;
these are the signs of one who is corrupted.
All rivers have a winding course,
all forests are made of wood,
and all women commit evil.
While obtaining a sheltered place—
if one could find a moment, or a private spot,
or even such a windless place as that;
Could every woman who commits evil find another [husband] even with one who is a cripple?
Among women who take delight in men—
Women who have many hearts and are unrestrained—
if they should fail to inspire affection in every respect,
one should not trust them, for women are like unstable ground.
Having abandoned such a mortal husband, whom even all the women of the Kaṇḍarī kinnaras find no pleasure in living with at home—
his wife, having left him, [goes forth].
Having seen another man, a cripple crawling on a wooden board,
the wife of King Bāvarika— the Bakas— was utterly devoted to sensual pleasures.
No woman ever transgressed against anyone other than her husband, who followed the lead of Paṭṭhava;
even Piṅgiyānī did not transgress against the Lord of the Entire World.
She was the beloved queen of King Brahmadatta;
yet she did not act according to the will of him who followed her wishes, nor did she, though desiring pleasure, ever obtain it from him.
A man who is not devoted to the gods [should avoid] those who are greedy, fickle-minded, ungrateful, and treacherous.
One should have faith in sloth.
They do not understand what has been done or what remains to be done,
nor do they recognize their mother, father, or brother.
The ignoble ones, having transcended the [true] Dhamma,
fall under the sway of their own minds,
even toward that which has long been familiar, dear, and pleasing.
They abandon even a husband who is compassionate toward them as their own life and who assists them in their household duties;
therefore, I do not trust women.
For the mind is indeed like a monkey,
like a tree's shadow reaching from ear to ear;
the heart of women is ever-shifting and unsteady.
It revolves like the rim of a wheel.
When they look upon it with longing,
seeing it as a desirable form, the wealth of a man;
The people of Kamboja lead him along with gentle words,
as one leads a horse with a lotus-flower;
when they look at him and do not see [any fault], they let him go.
A man’s wealth that is worthy of being accepted—
people avoid it from every side,
just as one who has crossed over and reached the far bank avoids a raft.
Like fire, they devour everything;
like rivers with swift currents, their deceit is sharp;
these [passions] pursue both the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Just as a boat [crosses] from this shore to the other,
it is not for one person alone nor for two;
it is like a marketplace laid out for sale.
Whoever should think "these are mine" would be trying to hold back the wind with a net;
they are like a river and a path.
The tavern, the assembly hall,
and the drinking house—
such are the women of the world; no limit for them exists.
These are like pots on their stands,
resembling the heads of black snakes;
they are like cattle in a field of abundant grass.
They choose one after another:
the elephant with its temple-juice flowing, the black serpent,
the consecrated king, and every beautiful woman.
A person should associate with these people constantly;
for their nature is indeed difficult to understand.
Though they possess a most beautiful appearance, they are not dear to many.
One should not consort with courtesans,
nor with another’s wife, nor for the sake of wealth—
these five kinds of women should not be consorted with.
Then, sirs, the vulture king Ānanda, having understood the beginning, middle, and end of the bird Kuṇāla’s discourse, at that time spoke these verses:
“Even this entire earth filled with wealth,
a man might give it to a woman who is highly esteemed;”
Even having gained such an opportunity, one should not despise it,
nor should one fall under the power of those unchaste women.
Even if she is industrious and her conduct is not lax...
Even the Prince Komārabhacca, beloved and pleasing,
they abandon when their dwelling duties are finished;
therefore, I do not trust women.
A person who desires counsel should not trust,
nor should he trust one who weeps in his presence;
for these serve both the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Just as a boat [crosses] from this shore to the other,
one should not trust a friend who was once an old enemy,
nor should one trust an old thief who was once a friend.
One should not trust a king, thinking, "He is my friend";
one should not trust a woman, thinking, "She is my mother.
One should not trust women who act like Rāma.
In women who are utterly unrestrained despite their vows of virtue,
a husband who is pursued by excessive love should not place his trust,
for such women are like those standing on the edge of a precipice.
They might tear them out, they might cut them off,
or even having cut them at the throat, they might drink the blood;
yet one should not [be attached] to those who desire base things and are unrestrained.
In their minds, they compare these things to the banks of the Ganges:
for them, what is false appears as true,
and for them, what is true appears as false.
Like cattle in a field of lush grass,
they graze upon the best and the finest;
lured by what has passed, they entice others.
By looking and by laughing,
and also by ill-cladness and by speaking softly.
These are the Coriyo, Kathino, Hetā,
Vāḷā, and Lapasakkharā;
they do not know nothing at all.
That which is deception among humans:
women in this world are indeed insatiable;
no limit for them exists.
Passionate and impudent,
like a fire that consumes everything—
there is no one called "dear" to women.
There is no one who is not dear;
these people serve both the dear and the not-dear,
just as a boat [crosses] from this shore to the other.
There is no one called "dear" among women,
nor does anyone exist who is not dear;
it is because of wealth that they are called "beloved."
Like a creeper depending on a tree:
the elephant-tether, the horse-tether,
the cow-pen, and the human circle.
Women follow after a man who is wealthy, even if he is one who burns his children and throws away flowers.
They abandon even a son of noble family if he is destitute.
"Even one who resembles a dog;
women follow and pursue him for the sake of wealth."
Then, sirs, Nārada the divine brahmin, having understood the beginning, middle, and end of Ānanda the king of vultures’ discourse, on that occasion recited these verses:
“Four things do not fulfill themselves;
listen to me as I speak of them:”
The ocean, the brahmin, the king,
the woman, and the lord of birds—
these rivers flow toward the sea.
Whatever rivers exist on earth,
they do not fill the ocean;
for it is because of its vastness that it is never filled.
And a Brahmin who has studied the Veda,
with narrative as the fifth constituent,
should desire to hear even more.
For what is deficient is not filled.
And the king [might rule] the entire earth,
together with its oceans and mountains;
Having conquered and dwelt [there],
he aspires for the further shore of the ocean, which is worthy of the most excellent jewels.
For when diminished, it is not filled.
If there were eight husbands for each single woman, [it still would not suffice].
Brave and powerful,
bringing forth the essence of all desires— one should apply one's will to the ninth [jhāna].
For when empty, it does not fill up.
All women are like fire, devouring everything;
all women are like rivers, carrying everything away.
All women are like the branches of thorny trees;
all women go for the sake of wealth.
It is as if a man were to try to grasp the wind with a net.
One might empty the ocean with a single hand;
one might make a sound with one's own hand—
but he who abandons every attachment to women [is truly great].
Among women who possess many wiles,
in whom truth is very hard to find,
the true nature of women is difficult to comprehend.
Like a fish gone into the water,
they are soft-spoken but inwardly burning;
difficult to satisfy, they are like rivers.
Knowing this, one should avoid it from afar;
for it is a great illusion that ensnares.
It is a corruption of the holy life; knowing this,
one should avoid it from afar.
Whomever they serve,
whether by desire or by wealth,
he stands firm like fire.
“They quickly burn you up.
Then, indeed, the bird Kuṇāla, having understood the beginning, middle, and end of Nārada the divine brahmin’s discourse, at that time spoke these verses:
“One may converse with one who holds a sharpened sword in hand;”
Even a wise man, though he might bite a goblin or a venomous serpent of fierce power,
would not speak alone with a single woman.
For women are indeed the churners of the world's hearts,
armed with the weapons of dance, song, and speech;
they afflict one whose mindfulness is not established.
Like a host of demons toward merchants on the island,
they have neither discipline nor restraint;
they are addicted to liquor and meat, lacking self-control.
They swallow up a man’s fortune,
as the timingala fish swallows the makara in the ocean;
they range through the enjoyment of the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Agitated, unstable, and unrestrained,
women rush toward those who are heedless,
just as waters flow into the salt sea.
The woman who seduces a man— whether by desire,
by pleasure, or by wealth— even if he is like the fire itself (jātavedasa),
such a person [is not truly led astray].
Those who have destroyed lust and hatred burn him down.
Seeing that a man is wealthy and possesses great riches,
they approach him along with their wealth and their wives.
They entwine his reddened heart,
just as the *māluva* creeper entwines a *sāla* tree in the forest;
they approach him with manifold desires.
Adorned with variegated masks,
these women laugh and mock, like Śambara himself,
who is skilled in a hundred deceptions.
Women adorned with gold, gems, and pearls,
honored in their own families,
will transgress against their husbands even when they are protected.
They dwell within his heart like a Dānava.
For even a man who is radiant and wise,
honored and revered by many people, [is not free from them].
Falling under the power of women, he does not speak,
like the moon eclipsed by Rāhu;
whatever he might do in anger toward this or that direction—
One who has fallen under the power of an enemy with a wicked mind meets with even greater calamity than that;
one who has fallen under the power of women, being full of longing, does not.
With hair shorn, nails clipped, and terrified,
beaten with feet, hands, and sticks—
the women indeed approached only what was base.
They delight in them like flies on carrion.
Whether among families or in the intervals between streets,
or again in royal capitals and market towns;
One who desires happiness, possessing the eye of wisdom, should avoid the snare set by Namuci;
having cast aside wholesome merit and the qualities of asceticism, [he would fall].
He who does not practice ignoble conduct will be led by the deities to hell,
like a merchant carrying a gem to a place where it is cut to pieces.
Thus, censured here and ruined in the next world by his own karma,
the fool goes to the Gaḷagaḷa hell, where there is no fixed end.
Like a vicious mule-cart on a wrong path,
he goes to the Patāpana hell,
as well as the Simbali forest of spears and the iron [hell].
Having dwelt in the animal realm,
one does not escape the domain of the King of the Petas;
nor does one find the divine play and delights in the Nandana grove.
Among humans, women destroy the conduct of a wheel-turning monarch when he is heedless,
and they lead him to an unhappy rebirth.
Divine pleasures and delights are not difficult to obtain,
nor is the conduct of a universal monarch among humans,
nor are celestial nymphs dwelling in golden mansions.
For those who wander seeking the destruction of negligence,
the state of transcending the realm of sense-desire is their destination;
for them, rebirth in the realm of form is not difficult to attain.
Those who, seeking to destroy intoxication,
practice for rebirth in the realm of those free from passion—
that auspicious state which transcends all suffering—
It is utterly unmoving and unconditioned;
it is not difficult for those who have attained purity to reach Nibbāna,
provided they wander seeking the destruction of passion.
“At that time I was Kuṇāla,
Udāyī was the Phussa cuckoo,
and Ānanda was the king of the vultures.”
Sāriputta was Nārada;
the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly—
thus you should remember this Jātaka.
The Kuṇāla Jātaka, the fourth.
